query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal oxidation treatment that forms a continuous, adherent lubricious oxide layer on the high-entropy alloy surface will lower both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate over a wide temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 or similar) produced with a native, non-optimized surface oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Apply a single-step thermal oxidation treatment in air at an optimized temperature and duration to promote the in‐situ formation of a protective lubricant oxide film.
generation.conditions: The treatment is designed to be effective across a broad service-temperature range (from room temperature to elevated temperatures, e.g., up to 300°C or higher) and under conditions where cyclic mechanical stresses are present.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, continuous, and adherent oxide layer (e.g., enriched in elements such as Ti or Cr, forming oxides like TiO2 or Cr2O3) that is self-healing under operating conditions.
generation.mechanism: The preformed oxide film acts as a solid lubricant by reducing shear stress during sliding contact and by providing a protective barrier that minimizes material removal, thereby reducing friction and wear. Its stability over a wide temperature range ensures sustained self-lubrication.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated alloys with only native oxides, the intervention is expected to reduce the coefficient of friction by roughly up to 50% and lower the wear rate by at least an order of magnitude under identical load conditions.
generation.baseline: The untreated high-entropy alloy exhibiting its as-fabricated or naturally oxidized surface, which has higher friction and wear rates under mechanical loading.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected to persist as long as the oxide layer remains continuous and adherent. If the oxide layer spalls or degrades due to excessive mechanical stress or aggressive chemical environments, the improvement may be diminished.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence indicates that protective oxide layers can enhance wear resistance at high temperatures, the optimal oxidation parameters and exact magnitude of friction and wear reduction across all service temperatures remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to the controlled thermal oxidation treatment to form the lubricious oxide layer, while keeping the other set as untreated controls. Conduct standardized reciprocating sliding wear tests across a range of temperatures (room temperature to elevated temperatures).
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) during sliding tests
Wear rate determined by volume loss measurements (e.g., via profilometry)
Surface characterization (e.g., SEM, XRD) to confirm the presence and integrity of the oxide layer before and after wear testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally oxidized samples do not exhibit a significantly lower COF (e.g., approximately 50% lower) and a substantially reduced wear rate (e.g., at least one order of magnitude lower) compared to the untreated controls across the tested temperature range, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening. Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
